summary:
The Maldives criminalises same-sex conduct and same-sex marriage under its Penal Code, whose amended provisions took effect in 2015. Section 131 defines criminal sexual contact as sexual contact without a reason permitted under Islamic law, and section 411(2) names same-sex intercourse as an offence under section 411(f). Section 410(a)(8), in force since 16 July 2015, criminalises marriage between two persons of the same sex. Penalties run to one year for unlawful marriage under section 410(a)(8), up to eight years for the conduct covered by sections 411(a)(2) and 411(d) with a supplementary 100 lashes available under Sharia, and up to four years for unlawful sexual conduct under section 412. The 2014 code extended the offence beyond Muslims to all persons.

Capital punishment is not available for these offences: the source states homosexual acts cannot be punished with death under Maldivian law, noting that executions have been suspended since 1953 and that under sections 92(k) and 1205 death is only available for egregious purposeful killing; plans to restart executions were later abandoned. Reporting in 2015 described death-penalty provisions as theoretically in reach for the offence, a claim the statute's own terms do not support.

Enforcement is documented in one instance: on 29 August 2015 police on Dhaandhoo arrested two local men, aged 56 and 27, for homosexual activity in a private home following a public complaint. The source describes prosecution as rare and homosexuality as a social taboo. The most recent documented enforcement case in this record is from 2015; no later instance is documented.

No transgender-specific criminal provision, document rule, screening rule, facility rule, custody rule or care rule is codified; all codified offences and penalties concern same-sex sexual activity and same-sex marriage. There is no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. The record contains no documented statement about societal treatment of transgender people as a distinct group; tolerance and hostility descriptions refer to LGBTQ persons generally, homosexuality, or homophobia.

UN mechanisms have flagged the regime. The Human Rights Committee recommended anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and action against stigmatisation of homosexuals, recorded in the OHCHR compilation for the Maldives' second-cycle UPR (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/2, March 2015). The Maldives rejected 60 UPR recommendations said to contradict the Islamic faith and the Constitution, including those relating to LGBT and non-traditional forms of the family, and noted but did not accept 2015 recommendations to decriminalise consenting adult same-sex relations. The government's own UPR report (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/1, April 2015) records that of 126 first-cycle recommendations it fully accepted 89, partially accepted 11, took note of 6 and rejected 20 with reasons. The Maldives signed the 2008 UN document opposing decriminalisation and rejected 2011 and September 2014 UN resolutions on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The UN Population Fund reported that those perceived as homosexual or transgender in the Maldives were targets of hate crimes and other human rights violations and recommended law reform; these recommendations were noted by the Maldives but not accepted. The HRMI Maldives Summary Report 2024 (second expert survey) found human-rights experts most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people, alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers, as at risk of empowerment-rights violations; political participation scored 6.4/10 while other civil and political rights scored considerably lower.

Documented violence includes the 2013 neck stabbing of gay blogger Hilath Rasheed in Male. In 2014 New Zealand granted asylum to gay Maldivian Abraham Naim as at risk of serious harm from state agents; a President's Office spokesman commented that those seeking asylum for sexual-orientation discrimination would face prosecution upon return. The 2020 US Country Reports found no reports of officials complicit in abuses against LGBTI persons, though societal stigma likely discouraged reporting, and recorded that local citizens expressing support for LGBTI rights on social media were targeted online as apostates or irreligious. Rainbow Warriors stated the local LGBTQ movement is mostly limited to the virtual world due to the intensity of homophobia, and warned tourists could face similar threats to those documented locally.

Private tourist islands, resorts and hotels are usually isolated from population centres and, as evidenced by alcohol sale, operate outside the reach of Islamic law in practice; LGBTQ tourists are generally considered welcome there. Outside tourist areas, guides advise caution regarding public displays of affection.
tangentialFactors:
The HRMI 2024 expert survey places LGBTQIA+ people among the groups most at risk of empowerment-rights violations in the Maldives, alongside migrants, journalists and religious minorities, with political participation scoring relatively better at 6.4/10 than other civil and political rights.

Raw-count context: the record documents one enforcement action (the 2015 Dhaandhoo arrests) and one violent incident (the 2013 stabbing of Hilath Rasheed). These are single cases, not rates, and cannot be compared across jurisdictions on magnitude.

The Maldives' reservations to the ICCPR, CEDAW and CRC, and concerns including sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage, are recorded in the UN UPR compilation of March 2015.

Residents face criminal liability under sections 410(a)(8), 411 and 412 of the Penal Code regardless of religion, the 2014 code having extended the offence beyond Muslims to all persons. Penalties reach eight years plus supplementary 100 lashes under Sharia for the conduct under sections 411(a)(2) and 411(d).

Local LGBTQ advocacy operates largely online, which Rainbow Warriors attributed to the intensity of homophobia. Citizens expressing support for LGBTI rights on social media have been targeted as apostates or irreligious, per the 2020 US Country Reports.
